title: What is Transfer Learning? Transfer Learning in Keras | Fine Tuning Vs Feature Extraction
full_text: Hi guys, my name is Nitesh and you are  welcome to CampusX. In this video, we  will continue our deep learning  playlist. And today's video topic is  very important and very interesting. In  today's video, you are going to learn  Transfer Learning, which is basically a  technique used in machine learning  where you train your model on one  dataset and then run it on another. And  this is a method that has become very  famous in the last five or six years.  And today, the biggest personalities in  deep learning say that transfer  learning will be the next big thing. So  that is why it is very important for  you to learn this. So in the video, I  will first try to explain everything  conceptually and theoretically, and  then in the second half of the video, I  will show you how to do transfer  learning in Keras. Okay? So, let's  start the video. Before starting  transfer learning, let's discuss what  the problem is if you go to train a  deep learning model from scratch. I  have told you multiple times in this  playlist that deep learning models are  data hungry. Which basically means that  if you want to train your own deep  learning model, you need a lot of  labeled data, which is costly. If you  want to build a cat-dog classifier, you  need lots of images, let's say 10,000  images. Now, you can scrape these  images from Google. But with every  image, you will also have to provide  the information about which image has a  cat and which has a dog. Now, this  labeling is difficult and you need  manual labor. Right? And this is costly . Companies have to pay money for this.  So the biggest problem that comes with  training your own deep learning model  is that you need a lot of data. If that  data is not publicly available, it will  take time and effort to create it. Okay ? Problem number two: Deep learning  models, especially if you are training  your model on a big dataset, take a lot  of time to get trained. It takes a lot  of time for a model to train. It could  be days or weeks, and in certain cases,  it could even take months. If your  dataset is very large. So this is the  second disadvantage. Because of these  two reasons, generally, people do not  prefer training their own deep learning  model that much. Okay? So if training  your own deep learning model is  difficult, then what is the solution?  The solution is using pretrained models . If you remember, a few days ago I  uploaded a video on my channel about  Pretrained Models in CNN. Where I told  you about the ImageNet dataset, which  is a very large dataset of images, a  dataset about daily objects and animals . This dataset has around 1.4 million  images of about 1000 classes, classes  like chairs, bread, and different dog  breeds. ImageNet is a dataset of this  kind, and a competition started being  organized on it named ILSVRC, okay,  ImageNet Large Scale Visual Recognition  Challenge, which began around 2010. And  in this video, I explained how, from  2012 onwards, some deep learning model  wins this competition every year. So in  this video, I explained to you that  these models that came and won this  competition, like VGG and ResNet and  InceptionNet, all these models are so  good and so well-trained on this data  that you can take them and use them in  your own projects too. And that is the  whole concept behind pretrained models.  So, a pretrained model is a CNN model  that has been trained on some other  data. Okay? And that dataset is large  enough to have all the categories. Now  what you can do is you can apply that  dataset to your own data. You can use  that same model in your project.  Because it has already learned from a  previous large dataset. Okay? So I  covered this entire thing in that video . This is the summary of that video. If  you haven't watched that video, I would  recommend it to you. You should  definitely go and watch it once. I am  putting its link in the description.  Please watch it once. Then it will be a  bit clearer to you what pretrained  models are and what their job is. Okay?  Now, in the code we wrote in the last  video, we had created a generic  classifier that was able to classify  any kind of object. If I remember  correctly, there I classified a chair,  classified bread, classified a dog, and  classified a tomato. So these are like  general objects. So, there can be a  problem with pretrained models as well,  and that problem is: what if the  project you are working on, your  pretrained model doesn't even know that  class? I will try to explain. Let's say  you are working specifically on phone  versus tablet classification. Okay?  Your task is to look at an image and  determine whether it contains a phone  or a tablet. And you decided to use VGG  Net as a pretrained model, which is  trained on the ImageNet dataset. Now,  what if neither phones nor tablets are  among these 1,000 classes in the  ImageNet dataset? Now that is an issue.  Everything we were classifying so far  fell within these 1,000 classes. And  that is why we were getting results.  But it is not necessary that whenever  you work on a project, you will always  have the same classes that are inside  these 1,000 classes. Now, this is the  problem that we are trying to solve.  And to solve this problem, we use  transfer learning, which is the topic  of today's video. Okay? So going  forward, what we will do is first learn  what transfer learning is, and then we  will implement it in code using Keras.  So first, I will try to explain to you  in very simple words what transfer  learning is. I have taken this  definition from Wikipedia. Let's read  it once. Transfer learning is a  research problem in machine learning  that focuses on storing knowledge  gained while solving one problem and  applying it to a different but related  problem. Okay? This is a simple  definition. But I will explain it a  little more. So, as I just told you,  what do you do? In pretrained models,  you try out a CNN trained on another  dataset on your own dataset, and you do  this because there are two benefits.  First, you don't need your own large  dataset, which is costly, and second,  it saves time. So, transfer learning  does exactly that for us. Okay? And  since 2015-16, transfer learning has  actually become a big deal in the  machine learning space. In fact, you  can see this chart. Here, Andrew Ng  said that if you remove supervised  learning, then in second place,  transfer learning is the thing that  will take machine learning forward in  the industry. Okay? You can see the  chart, even better than unsupervised  learning and reinforcement learning.  Okay? Now, such a sentiment is building  in the industry because transfer  learning solves your problem very  easily. Okay? So, if you think about it , what are you doing in transfer  learning? You are applying what you  have learned from another dataset to  your own dataset. Honestly speaking, we  do the same thing in real life as well.  This means that I want to say transfer  learning is actually inspired by real  life. I will give you some examples. So , why are you told that before riding a  motorcycle, you should know how to ride  a bicycle? Because what you are  effectively doing, what your brain is  doing, is that when you learn to ride a  bicycle, some learning happens in your  brain. Right? Some knowledge is formed.  Now, riding a motorcycle is a separate  task. But it is a related task. You  need balancing in both. So, if you have  learned to ride a bicycle, riding a  motorcycle will become a bit easier.  Because your brain will use the  knowledge it gained from riding the  bicycle to ride the motorcycle.  Similarly, let's say you know how to  play a musical instrument. Let's say a  violin or something. Then you will be  able to play a related instrument well  too. Let's say a guitar. Why? Because  you have an understanding of musical  notes. So you do this all the time:  applying knowledge from one domain to  another domain. Computer scientists  integrated this simple idea into deep  learning and machine learning, and this  is what is called transfer learning.  Right? Next, I will teach you exactly  how transfer learning works. What is  working under the hood. So, to  understand how transfer learning works,  let's take a small example. Suppose we  want to do cat-dog classification, and  to do this classification, we will use  a pre-trained model. VGG16, which is a  very famous pre-trained model. Now, you  can see the architecture of this model  in this diagram. You can clearly see  that there are two parts in this model.  So one part is this, which we call the  convolutional layer part, or sometimes  it is also called the convolutional  base. And then there is a second part  where you have your fully connected  layers and your output layer. We call  this the FC layers or the FC part. So  this part, the convolutional base, its  job is to—and obviously we are doing  an image classification task—From  within the image, extract spatial  information. Right? So an image is  basically a 2D matrix of pixels. Right?  So what is the relationship between  these pixels in 2D is what our  convolutional base captures. And this  fully connected part, its job is to  perform classification. So this model,  VGG16, is trained on the ImageNet  dataset, which has 1000 classes. So  basically, it has learned on a  multi-class classification problem. And  you can see here that in the output,  there are 1000 nodes with Softmax  applied. Okay? Now, for a moment, let's  assume that these cat and dog classes  are not among those 1000. So let's  discuss how we apply transfer learning.  So what you will do is break this CNN  from this point. Okay? You keep this  part. The convolutional base, and you  remove this part. Okay? Then what you  do is, here is your convolutional base.  Now, you add your own dense layers or  FC layers on top of it as per your  needs. Like there were three dense  layers here. You can add as many as you  want, and you also decide how many  neurons each dense layer will have. And  finally, you put an output layer with  one neuron. Because what we are doing  now is a binary classification problem,  and you apply Sigmoid there. Also, what  you do is you freeze this convolutional  layer, this convolutional base.  Freezing means that when you retrain  this entire network, only this part  will be trained. This part will not be  trained. And then you train the model  on whatever data you have. Suppose you  have even a little bit of data, even  100 images each. Then what do you do?  You train this model on your small  amount of data. This part does not get  trained. This part gets trained. And  that's it. That is what transfer  learning is. So what you are  essentially doing is using the  knowledge that was already learned in  this part on ImageNet and applying it  to your task. Okay? So this is the main  idea. This is how transfer learning  works. Okay? Now I will explain to you  next why the thing you just learned  works. So let me explain why transfer  learning works. For that, let's revise  it once again. What we just studied  about how transfer learning works. So  what you do is, you are working on a  problem. Let's say you want to do  cat-dog classification and for that,  you choose the VGG16 model which is  already trained on the ImageNet dataset . So what you do is, you remove this  dense part, the dense layer part. Okay?  And you replace it with your own dense  layers where you can add any number of  layers. You can add any number of  neurons. And in the end, there is a  single neuron which is your output  layer because you are going to do  binary classification. And you attach  them in this way. Also, what you do is  you freeze this convolutional base  layer. So that the weight values here  do not change. Because the true  knowledge is hidden in the weight  values. Which this VGG16 had learned.  While getting trained on ImageNet. Okay ? And you train this entire  architecture again on your small  dataset. Nothing changes in this part.  And here, you learn the weights. And  that is how transfer learning works.  Okay? Now let's try to understand why  this technique is working. Why is it  able to give results? The answer is  very simple. If you remember, we  discussed at the very beginning of CNN  that when you add so many convolution  layers, the job of these convolution  layers is to decode the image and, in a  way, extract features to see what is in  the image. And then the layers that  follow have the job of doing the  classification. Now, we also discussed  that your early layers, the initial  layers, have the job of extracting  primitive features like edges. As you  go to deeper layers, you extract more  complex patterns and features. Like  shapes. Okay? And then gradually, you  eventually create features and pass  them on. So the concept is very simple.  The concept is that your ImageNet  dataset contains data related to around  1000 classes. Now take anything that  exists in the real world. Its primitive  features will be similar. They are  general. Okay? They will definitely  have edges. They will definitely have  shapes. That is why we decided that the  things learned at the beginning are  kind of common for all tasks, for all  image classification tasks, so there is  no need to learn them again. So that is  why we used this entire convolutional  base exactly as it is. And then for the  specific classification task ahead, we  added our own layers and retrained the  entire model. So that is why transfer  learning works. Because when you train  this model for the first time, it has  already learned the primitive and  general features during the training  process. There is no need to do that  work again. Okay? So basically, the  whole principle behind this entire  thing is: do not reinvent the wheel.  Don't build the wheel over and over. If  the wheel is already made, use it to  build a car. Okay? I hope you  understood the idea. So next, we will  learn about the different ways to apply  transfer learning. There are precisely  two ways. Okay? I will tell you the  names of both. The first method is  called feature extraction. And the  second one is fine-tuning. Now, this  feature extraction is exactly what we  just discussed, where you replace the  last dense layers with your own dense  layers, freeze the convolutional base,  and retrain the model on your data.  This is what is called feature  extraction. Okay? Feature extraction is  generally done when the labels in the  image classification task you are  working on are somewhat similar to the  data on which your model is already  trained. For example, if you are doing  dog vs. cat classification, you should  use feature extraction. Why? Because  training on animals has already been  done in ImageNet. So you know that the  layers up to this point have already  learned to recognize animals or their  features. Okay? So you only need to  make changes to the last layers.  Whereas in fine-tuning, you also  retrain some of the last convolutional  layers. You don't freeze them. So you  freeze the layers from here to here.  But you unfreeze the last layers. And  you add your own dense layers. And then  you retrain this entire part. You  retrain this entire part. When should  you apply fine-tuning? It is very  simple. If you are working on a problem  that is very different from your  dataset's classification labels. Let's  say, all of a sudden, I am trying to do  a classification between phones versus  tablets. And for a moment, let's assume  that ImageNet did not have any data  even remotely like this. So, even then,  I can reuse the initial layers. Because  these contain very primitive features.  But as you move forward, the knowledge  in those layers is slightly different  from my requirements. So that is why  what I would like to do is, I will... unfreeze the last few layers and  retrain the model entirely. Obviously,  it will take a little more time in this  case, but you would see you get better  results. Okay?
